cards.question: What is Node.js?
cards.answer: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime for executing JS outside the browser. Used for creating servers, CLI tools, bots, scripts. Uses Chrome's V8 engine. Has built-in modules (fs, http, path). npm ecosystem with millions of packages.
keyPoints: JavaScript runtime outside the browser (based on Chrome's V8 engine)
Single-threaded with non-blocking I/O and Event Loop
Used for servers, CLI, scripts
npm ecosystem — largest package registry

cards.question: How does Node.js's asynchronous model work?
cards.answer: Node.js uses Event Loop for async processing. Non-blocking I/O — operations run in background. Callbacks, Promises, async/await for handling results. EventEmitter for events system. Allows handling thousands of connections simultaneously.
keyPoints: Event Loop — event processing cycle (single-threaded)
Non-blocking I/O — operations run in background (libuv)
Callbacks, Promises, async/await for handling results
Can handle thousands of connections simultaneously

cards.question: What is CommonJS and how do require/module.exports work?
cards.answer: CommonJS is Node.js module standard. require('./file.js') imports a module. module.exports = { func } exports. Synchronous import. Each file is a separate module. Module variables are private, not visible outside. Old format but still popular.
keyPoints: require() — synchronous module import
module.exports — export from module
Each file is a separate module with private scope
Modules are cached after first require

cards.question: What is the difference between require and import?
cards.answer: require (CommonJS) — synchronous, dynamic, for Node.js. import (ES6) — asynchronous, static, standard. import can be analyzed at build time. require allows dynamic paths. Modern Node.js supports import with 'type': 'module' in package.json.
keyPoints: require — synchronous, dynamic (CommonJS)
import — statically analyzed, ES Modules standard
import allows tree-shaking during build
Node.js supports ESM via type: 'module' in package.json

cards.question: What built-in Node.js modules do you know?
cards.answer: fs — working with files and folders. http — HTTP server. https — HTTPS. path — working with paths. events — EventEmitter. stream — data streams. os — OS information. util — utilities. child_process — running subprocesses. crypto — cryptography.
keyPoints: fs — filesystem operations (sync and async API)
http/https — creating HTTP servers and requests
path — safe working with file paths
events — EventEmitter, stream — streaming data processing
child_process — running subprocesses, crypto — cryptography

cards.question: How do you create a simple HTTP server in Node.js?
cards.answer: const http = require('http'); const server = http.createServer((req, res) => { res.end('Hello'); }); server.listen(3000); Use frameworks for real applications: Express, Fastify, Hapi, Koa. Routing, middleware, authentication — all in frameworks.
keyPoints: http.createServer() with callback (req, res)
server.listen(port) to start
For real applications — use frameworks (Express, Fastify)
Frameworks add routing, middleware, error handling

cards.question: Which framework should you choose for a Node.js server?
cards.answer: Express — most popular, simple, large community. Fastify — faster, modern. Hapi — enterprise, lots built-in. Koa — compact, uses async/await. Choose depending on project. For beginners: Express. For production: Fastify or Hapi.
keyPoints: Express — most popular, simple, huge ecosystem
Fastify — high performance, schema validation, modern
Koa — minimal, async/await, from Express creators
Choice depends on project requirements and team

cards.question: What are Streams in Node.js and what types exist?
cards.answer: Streams are a way to process data in chunks without loading everything into memory. 4 types: Readable (read, fs.createReadStream), Writable (write, fs.createWriteStream), Duplex (read and write, net.Socket), Transform (transform, zlib.createGzip). Use pipe() to connect: readable.pipe(transform).pipe(writable).
keyPoints: Process data in chunks, don't load everything in memory
4 types: Readable, Writable, Duplex, Transform
pipe() to connect streams in a chain
Efficient for large files and network data

cards.question: How do you properly handle errors in Node.js? What is uncaughtException?
cards.answer: Sync errors — try/catch. Async — .catch() for promises, error event for streams. process.on('uncaughtException') catches unhandled exceptions — must log and exit. process.on('unhandledRejection') for promises. In Express — error middleware (err, req, res, next). Always log errors, never swallow them silently.
keyPoints: try/catch for sync code, .catch() for promises
process.on('uncaughtException') — catches unhandled exceptions
process.on('unhandledRejection') — unhandled promise rejections
On uncaughtException must log and exit (graceful shutdown)
In Express — error middleware with 4 args (err, req, res, next)

cards.question: What are Worker Threads and child_process? What's the difference?
cards.answer: child_process.fork() creates a new Node.js process with separate memory — communicate via IPC (message passing). Worker Threads (worker_threads) — threads in one process with shared memory (SharedArrayBuffer). Workers are lightweight, good for CPU tasks (parsing, computations). child_process for isolation and running external commands. Cluster module uses fork to scale HTTP server to all cores.
keyPoints: child_process.fork() — new process with separate memory, IPC communication
Worker Threads — threads in one process, shared memory (SharedArrayBuffer)
Workers are lightweight, good for CPU-intensive tasks
Cluster module — scale HTTP server to all CPU cores
